Red-tailed Hawk, Bald Eagle, Orchard Oriole, and Common Raven all successfully nest in a one mile stretch from the Route 30 Bridge to the Blackbridge Railroad Bridge. In winter over a dozen waterfowl species have been recorded here including Common Goldeneye, Canvasback, Bufflehead, American Black Duck, Redhead, Wood Duck, and (a rarity in York) Trumpeter Swan. On the fringe of migration season cormorants, grebes, and others stop along the creek. If conditions are right and mud is exposed shorebirds have been viewed here Killdeer and Spotted Sandpiper are most common, but other species have been viewed. The long walk or bike along the NE Ext to Rudy Park gives a birder chances to view the following birds in the breeding season Wild Turkey, Wood Thrush, Great Egret, Great Crested Flycatcher, Scarlet Tanager, and many other woodland birds. Though not an all season birding hot spot like the northern portion of the rail trail the stretch of trail from Brillhart Station parking area to Hanover Junction Train Station is good birding. The distance between these locations is over 6 miles, but the stretch has wooded and open habitats that are productive. The area between Glatfelters Station and Brillhart Station near the Howard Tunnel is great for woodland species and Louisiana Waterthrush in spring. Rusty Blackbird has been viewed at the edge of wet fields near Brillhart Station. A short walk south from Glatfelters Station parking look for Tree and Barn Swallows. Hanover Junction is famous for its Eastern Screech-Owl that year after year defends the creek alongside Great Blue Herons and Belted Kingfishers. Farther south to the Maryland line more chances for birds of open areas occur near Glen Rock as one heads south to New Freedom. Rough-legged Hawk was recorded near Glen Rock in a past Christmas bird count. The trail is long and stretches over half the county making it a trail that has had plenty of amazing bird sightings since its opening in 1999. Not all the parking information for all rail trail sections is included please visit the York County Parks webpage for more information.

properties.name: York Haven Hydro Dam
properties.property_manager: Cube Hydro Manager LLC and PA Fish and Boat Commission (814) 643-1831
properties.address: 100 Hydro Park Dr, York Haven, PA 17370
properties.parking: There is one small parking area by the dam and a small park beside the plant.
properties.restrooms: Restroom not available.
properties.safety_reminders: Please be aware of your surroundings and practice smart birding, it is not advisable to kayak or boat here without prior experience or knowledge of this section of river. Birding from shore is best. There is a portage ramp north of the dam behind the small park.
properties.best_birding: Non-waterfowl birding is best April through September, dawn until dusk. Waterfowl is best October-March.
properties.description: The York Haven Hydro Dam is quite popular among anglers, but the small park and views of the river make it a good birding spot. One of the best birding locales in York County was the nearby Brunner's Island Wetland which was recently closed to public access when management changed at that facility. The dam sits just north of Brunner's Island. A smaller island visible and close to the parking area at York Haven Hydro to the south of the dam on the east bank of the narrow Conewago Creek can hold some of the same woodland birds Brunner's was loved for. The Conewago Creek enters the river just below the dam and is a popular fishing spot. Listen for a Lousiana Waterthrush or Prothonotary Warbler here in the warmer months. The nearby Gut Road connecting Brunner's Island and Saginaw is also a nice place to look for woodland species that are present on Brunner's Island. Winter time waterfowl and gulls are possible here (typically in flyby form). A scope can help you scan the river. A canoe portage ramp behind the park near the railroad tracks affords a nice look north of the river. Please stay off the ramp and view birds off to the side. This way the ramp can be used for its primary function of assisting boaters around the dam. The small park gives good views of the tower above the dam which has had nesting Osprey in the past. Peregrine Falcon and Bald Eagle are also active in this area. In addition to raptors, the park often boasts a few Eastern Bluebirds, Tree Swallows, and Northern Mockingbirds. Large roosts of Black Vultures and Turkey Vultures occur nearby as well. Even if the park is quiet usually the skies above it are active. The York Haven Hydro area will not ever be the habitat that the Brunner's Island wetland area is, but it is still a good location to bird in Northeastern York County. Rarities and uncommon birds from the closed off wetland area included Least Bittern, shorebirds, and warbler species. Breeding Prothonotary Warblers were present here in good numbers, and certainly some of the spill over from this still present (yet posted) habitat can be viewed in the woods near the dam.

properties.name: Codorus Creek Game Lands
properties.restrooms: No facilities are available at the birding access points. Accessibility : Easy to moderate. SGL 416 is particularly well suited to short birding visits of an hour or less. None of the locations described here requires a long hike, and productive birding often begins immediately at the parking area. Woodberry offers the longest recommended walk, descending through a wooded creek valley before reaching open fields. Some field paths elsewhere in the Game Lands are periodically mowed but can become tall or overgrown during the growing season.
properties.description: State Game Lands 416 , also known as the Indian Rock Dam , Codorus Creek , or York New Salem Game Lands , protects 1,558 acres of fields, shrubland, wetlands, creek corridor, and woodland west of York. SGL 416 is somewhat unique among Pennsylvania State Game Lands. Rather than being state-owned, the property originated as part of a federal flood-control project and is owned by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, with much of the land managed for wildlife by the Pennsylvania Game Commission. Despite its size and proximity to York, it remains a relatively hidden and lesser-known public-access area. Following the devastating 1933 Codorus Creek flood, Congress authorized Indian Rock Dam in 1936, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers completed the project in 1942. Indian Rock is a dry flood-control dam: under normal conditions Codorus Creek flows through the project, but during major floods water can be temporarily stored across the broad valley upstream. The flood-control reservoir can hold approximately 9.1 billion gallons of water. Much of this federally owned flood-storage area is managed for wildlife by the Pennsylvania Game Commission as SGL 416. The result is a diverse patchwork of grass and forb fields, brushy early-successional habitat, hedgerows, seasonal wetlands, riparian woodland, mature forest, and Codorus Creek. The landscape is actively managed and changes over time. The Indian Rock management plan identifies approximately 350 acres for prescribed-fire management. Burning and other habitat-management practices help prevent some open areas from developing into continuous forest while encouraging grasses, wildflowers, shrubs, and young growth. This shifting mixture of habitats supports an equally diverse bird community. Birding Suggestions Unlike a park with a developed trail network, SGL 416 is best explored as a series of short birding stops. Each access point provides a somewhat different combination of habitats, and all can be worthwhile even when you have only a short time to bird. Site 1 - Sunnyside Road: Meadows, Wetlands & Codorus Creek → e Bird Hotsp ot Page The Sunnyside Road lot is the best-known birding location within SGL 416 and the site featured in the original York County Birding Trail. Its combination of meadow, hedgerows, seasonal wetland, mature trees, and Codorus Creek produces an impressive variety of birds. The eBird hotspot has documented 160 taxa. Birding Suggestions Begin birding as soon as you park. Explore the fields and hedgerows west of Sunnyside Road and check the mature trees surrounding the openings. During spring and summer, look and listen for Willow Flycatcher, Indigo Bunting, Eastern Towhee, Common Yellowthroat, Field Sparrow, Gray Catbird, and other birds of open and shrubby habitat. Willow Flycatcher is particularly well represented in the site's eBird records. The mature trees and woodland edges can be excellent for migrant warblers and vireos. Woodpecker diversity is also unusually good; Red-headed Woodpecker has been recorded repeatedly in addition to the more common woodpecker species. Pay particular attention to the low wet area near the parking lot. Depending on recent rainfall, it can range from nearly dry to shallow standing water. When flooded, it has produced Wood Duck, Hooded Merganser, Wilson's Snipe, Solitary Sandpiper, and even Sora , along with other migrant waterbirds. Walk along Sunnyside Rd toward the bridge and check Codorus Creek for Wood Duck, Great Blue Heron, Green Heron, Belted Kingfisher, and other creekside birds. Wood Duck is recorded regularly here from late winter through summer. In winter and during migration, carefully work the fields and brush for sparrows and other open-country birds. This is an excellent quick-check location. Even 30-60 minutes can cover several different habitats. Site 2 - Woodberry Road: Creek Valley, Woodland & Fields → e Bird Hotspot Page The Woodberry Road lot offers perhaps the most complete birding walk within SGL 416 and can easily occupy an hour or more if you follow the trail all the way through the wooded valley to the open fields. Birding Suggestions From the parking area, take the trail downhill into a forested creekside valley. Bird slowly on the descent-the sheltered woods and stream corridor provide some of the best woodland habitat among the recommended locations. Check the creek and quiet pools for Wood Duck, which has been recorded repeatedly here in spring. During migration, carefully work the wooded valley for warblers, vireos, thrushes, and flycatchers. Records include Wood Thrush, Acadian Flycatcher, Eastern Wood-Pewee, Great Crested Flycatcher, and several vireos. Watch dead trees, snags, and open portions of the woods for Red-headed Woodpecker, which has been recorded here repeatedly. Eventually the route emerges into open fields and brushy edge habitat. The bird community changes noticeably here. Look for Field Sparrow, Eastern Towhee, Indigo Bunting, Common Yellowthroat, and Yellow-breasted Chat . Both Baltimore and Orchard Orioles are also well represented in the eBird records. American Woodcock The open fields along Indian Rock Dam Road near the Woodberry lot have been a reliable location for American Woodcock in late winter and early spring. The eBird data strongly support this, with Woodcock reported repeatedly during its late-winter/early-spring display period. Visit around dusk from late February through March and listen for the male's nasal "peent" followed by its spiraling aerial display. Site 3 - Graybill Road: Woodland, Field & Forest Edge eBird Hotspot The Graybill Road pull-off is a less-established birding location but provides convenient access to another useful combination of habitats. There are two parking areas along Graybill: one is a parking lot surrounded by an open field, the other is a pull-off in a wooded area on the north side of Graybill. The parking lot area borders an open field, so spend some time scanning before entering the woods. During migration and winter, watch for open-country raptors. The habitat has potential for Northern Harrier, and the broad fields are also worth checking around dusk for Short-eared Owl, particularly during the colder months. These should be considered possibilities rather than expected birds. From either parking spot, walk along Graybill briefly to a pull-off area with a yellow gate. Walking down this gated road (Old Joseph Rd) goes through fields with well established hedgerows that can be productive. From the wooded pull-off area, a short trail on the north side of Graybill Road enters woodland. The route isn't long, making this another excellent place for a quick 30-60 minute stop. Birding Suggestions During spring and fall migration, walk the wooded section slowly and listen for warblers, vireos, thrushes, and flycatchers. Records from the limited eBird coverage include Wood Thrush, Eastern Wood-Pewee, Great Crested Flycatcher, and Red-eyed Vireo , along with several woodpeckers. Red-headed Woodpecker has been found here on multiple visits and is worth watching for around mature trees, snags, and more open woodland. Around the woodland edges and more open areas, listen for Field Sparrow, Eastern Towhee, Common Yellowthroat, Indigo Bunting, and other edge birds. Additional Areas to Explore Old Joseph Road Old Joseph Road provides a particularly interesting option for birders who don't mind rougher access. The road is rugged and and eventually dead-ends at the former Codorus Creek crossing, where there is ample place to park. If you park near the old creek crossing, you can retrace your path and walk along the road that you drove on...…or you can continue walking along Old Joseph Road away from the creek until reaching the powerline corridor. This provides another habitat transition worth exploring. Trinity Road The Trinity Road lot, near the Graybill Road intersection, provides another convenient place for a short check of fields, brush, and woodland edge. In late fall and winter, there can be a good sparrow diversity, including Field, American Tree, Fox, White-crowned, White-throated, Song, Lincoln's, and Swamp Sparrows . Indigo Bunting, Common Yellowthroat, Eastern Towhee, and Gray Catbird further reflect the early-successional habitat, while several woodpeckers and migrant woodland birds have also been recorded. Scan the fields for Northern Harrier in the winter. W. College Ave You can access the area on either side of W College Ave. There is a short loop you can take on the south side of the road which borders a field with a wooded river corridor area. On the north side of W. College Ave (the parking lot side), there is a larger field area that can be explored. Best Seasons Spring (March-May): Excellent. Begin with American Woodcock around Woodberry in late winter and early spring. As April and May progress, migrant warblers, vireos, thrushes, and flycatchers move through the wooded corridors, while flooded areas at Sunnyside can attract ducks, shorebirds, and rails. Summer (June-July): Excellent for breeding birds of fields, shrubland, woodland edge, and riparian habitat. Look for Indigo Bunting, Common Yellowthroat, Field Sparrow, Eastern Towhee, Yellow-breasted Chat, and orioles. Woodberry and Sunnyside provide particularly good opportunities to experience several habitat types in one visit. Fall (September-October): Excellent for migrant songbirds and sparrows. Concentrate on hedgerows, woodland edges, riparian trees, and brushy field margins. Old Joseph and Trinity can be particularly interesting for sparrows. Winter (November-February): Although quieter overall, the extensive fields make SGL 416 worth checking for sparrows and open-country raptors. Scan the larger fields around Graybill and elsewhere for Northern Harrier and the possibility of Short-eared Owl , while Codorus Creek and flooded areas can continue to produce waterbirds.

properties.name: Highpoint Scenic Vista & Recreation Area
properties.parking: There is one small parking area on Hilts Road.
properties.restrooms: There is a portable toilet at the parking area.
properties.safety_reminders: Please stay on the designated trails.
properties.best_birding: All seasons, dawn until dusk.
properties.description: At Highpoint the Heritage Trail is an ADA accessible climb to the top of the large hill that the park is named for. This trail is great for birding the open areas of the park. The vista sits 772' above sea level and gives visitors a view of the Susquehanna River. Highpoint lies further back from the river than Wrightsville and Apollo County Park which are both within binocular reach of the river. At Highpoint birders can look for river bound flyovers, but the appeal for birders is the 79 acres of meadowlands. The meadow has a draw during each season. Spring and early summer is the time when Horned Larks, Grasshopper Sparrows, and Savannah Sparrows can be heard singing alongside the path. Fall winds and rains switch to opportunities for swallows and American Pipit, and on sunny days migrating raptors like Northern Harrier and American Kestrel. Winter time sets up well for larger numbers of Horned Larks. In past years, a gravel and grit path would attract larks and this gave chances for their flock mates (buntings, pipits, and longspurs) when snow was melting off it. The surface of the path has changed, but the birds may still be viewed taking grit from Knights View Road. Early spring Late February through Mid-March, there is a chance to see the American Woodcock's winnow display just before dusk. Don't hike in too far just enough to reach the Mason-Dixon trail as it crosses the ADA loop. Here set up and look along the edge of the woods. Then look up and listen for the displaying birds. Be sure to leave the park before it is dark (park rules). You will only be able to see the display if there is enough light. Later in spring there are chances along the edges for Blue Grosbeak. The bird is typically viewed there in early May. The lower meadow loop (grass trail) is best to get to the areas along the woods edge that appeal to the Grosbeak. Around this time Grasshopper Sparrows are also returning. There are always birds at highpoint. The property is deceptively large. Birds often flush away from observers here, so just like at any other location patience pays off!

properties.name: West Manheim Township Park
properties.parking: There is a large stone parking lot that is available at the end of the stone driveway.
properties.restrooms: There is a portable toilet available in the back of the parking area.
properties.safety_reminders: Please practice good birding habits at this multi-use community park.
properties.best_birding: Birding is best May through October, dawn until dusk.
properties.description: This park has a small meadow, edge habitat, open forest, and is surrounded by agricultural fields. The area is lightly visited by birders. It is a popular recreation location with two multipurpose ball fields, playgrounds, a 5 acre dog park, and horseshoe pits. In addition to birding the trails are used for hiking, running, and mountain biking. According to the township's website future plans for the park include disk golf, and additional ball fields, volleyball courts, and pavilions. Upon entering the park you will see the meadows that run from the road to a hedgerow. There are trails through this area. A Purple Martin nesting house is active in the warm months. By mid-May the birds are easily viewed foraging for insects over the meadow near the park's entrance. The martin house is on private property, but the martins and other swallows often forage over the meadow each morning. It is likely the best public area for viewing martins in the county. The park has trails through open woods. Red-headed Woodpecker breeds in this area. Orchard Oriole is common in the hedgerows. There are a decent amount of cherry trees which tend to have many caterpillars feeding on them. This makes the area good for vireos, warblers, and cuckoos. During the summer Blue Grosbeak, Yellow Warbler, Grasshopper Sparrow, and more await in this small community park. Winter and fall are less birdy, but Fox Sparrow and other winter visitors are possible here. Another advantage of birding at West Manheim Township Park is its proximity to Sheppard-Meyers Reservoir and Long Arm Reservoir. Even if you don't have time to visit the lakes, many flyover waterfowl species and raptors are possible here because of the parks position between the two reservoirs.

properties.name: State Game Lands 242
properties.address: (242 Shooting Range) 1890 State Rte 4026, Dillsburg, PA 17019, (turn left onto Old Mountain Road to find the areas mentioned before arriving at the Shooting Range) There are several accesses on Game Road, Old Mountain Road and Old York Road.
properties.parking: At SGL 242 there are a dozen parking areas. Download the map from https://www.pgc.pa.gov/HuntTrap/StateGameLands/Documents/SGL%20Maps/SGL__242.pdf
properties.restrooms: Restrooms are not available.
properties.safety_reminders: Do not bird in these locations during popular hunting periods. Be smart always wear blaze orange if you choose to bird this property (as typically some game is in season throughout the year). It is required by law to wear fluorescent orange hat and vest when you are in gamelands from November 15-December 15th. First Sunday of rifle season is open to hunting do not go birding on this date. Some areas are posted March 1-June 15th for no entry, please follow all posted signs. Do not park in "no parking areas" or interfere with those hunting. Familiarize yourself with rules as the Game Commission may allow Sunday hunting soon. In the future one may even need a permit for non-hunting activities (not needed at this time).
properties.best_birding: Sundays and not during popular game seasons. Dawn until dusk.
properties.description: This area is managed by the PA Game Commission. The large property is 1,531 acres, located in Warrington and Carrol Townships. The terrain in the forest portions is quite hilly. Field habitat is present with different plantings in each field. The highest point is near Nell's Hill at 1,325 ft above sea level. It is one of the highest points in the county. Beaver Creek runs through the lowlands of the property and there is a large pond with limited seasonal access for viewing waterbirds. The blue-blazed Mason-Dixon Trail also runs through this property as it does five of the other locations on York County's Birding Map. One can begin birding SGL 242 by checking the fields near the Old York Road parking lots. Parking area 242-15 is good for this. Without using any trails a listener in the parking area will hear (in addition to traffic noise) summer time songs from Indigo Bunting, Common Yellowthroat, and Eastern Towhees in the hedgerows. Fall and winter blackbirds and sparrows are typically here in modest numbers. For those looking for adventure, quieter roads, and the best birding this property has to offer, turn on to Old Mountain Road from Old York Road. The next 3 areas require a bit of hiking (some on the Mason-Dixon Trail) to get into some of the habitat. This should only be attempted on Sundays or non-hunting days. At 242-35, the closest parking area on Old Mountain Road to Old York Road, you will find a power line cut, field, forest, and pond. The field, power line, and forest are accessible during spring migration, but the pond is closed off from March 1st-June 15th. The pond area has potential in the late summer and early fall for a lot of great birds. The area may provide stop over habitat for Sora, Virginia Rail, Bitterns, Herons, small pond ducks, and wetland songbirds. There is no full walking loop around the pond. As a hiker out and back is your best option. The field which is north of the pond is always worth a short hike for grassland birds and Ring-necked Pheasant. Red-tailed Hawk is common here. There is a short trail through the field. Mar-June 15th take a left at the yellow posted no entry sign to avoid going into the pond area, this will take you into the field. A short drive to parking area 242-40 gives you a chance to explore a field edged by a large conifer stand. Cross old mountain road and hike behind the gate along the wide path. The conifer stand in the back is worth scanning for Great Horned Owl and other raptors. The Mason-Dixon Trail can also be picked up here at the edge of the conifers. Hiking west on the trail you will cross Old Mountain Road and head up the hill through a forest with a decent amount of mature American Beech which is not that typical in this part of York. Within the forest Eastern Wood-Pewee, Red-eyed Vireo, and breeding Ovenbird are common. Cerulean Warbler and other uncommon to rare warblers are reported during migration occasionally in this forest. This same route (away from the steep downhill) takes you towards parking area 242-55 which is on the western edge of the property. Hiking down the steep hill and to the east will take you to another field on the property of SGL 242. Lastly park at 242-55 (off of Old Mountain Road near its intersection with Robson Road) hike uphill on a wide path from the parking area into an open forest. Red-headed Woodpeckers nest in this area. Other open forest birds including Eastern Bluebird are viewed here. The Mason-Dixon Trail goes by near the top of the hill. It is visible after walking a moderate distance from the parking area. You can continue east to reach the "Beech forest" and conifers mentioned earlier, but that hike is about a mile to the previous location near the conifers. It is hilly and about an hour in length depending on your speed. Please remember on State Game Lands birding is a lawful recreational activity, but it should be practiced safely and responsibly. Do not bird here when hunters are using the property for its primary purpose. Wear blaze orange. Sundays and non-hunting season days are acceptable times to bird SGL 242.
